definition: An artificial intelligence safety institute is a type of state-backed organization aiming to evaluate and ensure the safety of advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models, also called frontier AI models.
details: AI safety gained prominence in 2023, notably with public declarations about potential existential risks from AI. During the AI Safety Summit in November 2023, the United Kingdom and the United States both created their own AISI. During the AI Seoul Summit in May 2024, international leaders agreed to form a network of AI Safety Institutes, comprising institutes from the UK, the US, Japan, France, Germany, Italy, Singapore, South Korea, Australia, Canada and the European Union. In 2025, the UK's AI Safety Institute was renamed the "AI Security Institute", and its US counterpart became the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI).

explainer.lead: An artificial intelligence safety institute is a state-backed body that evaluates advanced, or frontier, AI models and works to ensure their safety. These institutes matter because they give governments dedicated organizations for examining powerful AI systems and cooperating across borders.

tiers.eli5: An AI safety institute is like a government-supported inspection team for very powerful computer programs. It checks whether advanced AI models are safe instead of simply assuming that they are. Different countries have created their own institutes, and many have agreed to connect them in an international network.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers should understand an AISI as a state-backed organization concerned with evaluating frontier AI models, not as a software package or evaluation algorithm. When working with institute publications or requirements, identify the relevant country and use the institute’s current name: the UK body became the AI Security Institute in 2025, while the US body became CAISI. International coordination also means that developments may involve several national institutes rather than one global authority.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, an AISI is a state-backed organization whose objectives are to evaluate and help ensure the safety of advanced AI models, also termed frontier AI models. The term denotes an institutional category rather than a particular evaluation method, metric, or technical standard. Its international form includes cooperation among national and regional institutes through the network agreed at the AI Seoul Summit in May 2024.

explainer.example: During the AI Safety Summit in November 2023, both the United Kingdom and the United States created an AISI. In 2025, the UK institute was renamed the AI Security Institute, and the US institute became the Center for AI Standards and Innovation.

usedIn.name: UK AI Security Institute
usedIn.detail: Created as the UK AI Safety Institute during the November 2023 AI Safety Summit and renamed in 2025.

usedIn.name: US Center for AI Standards and Innovation
usedIn.detail: The US counterpart created in November 2023, which became CAISI in 2025.

usedIn.name: International network of AI Safety Institutes
usedIn.detail: Agreed at the May 2024 AI Seoul Summit, linking institutes from participating countries and the European Union.

explainer.intuition: The basic idea is to give advanced AI safety a dedicated public institution, much as other consequential technologies can have specialized state-backed oversight and evaluation. An AISI focuses on frontier models rather than representing AI safety work in general.
howItWorks: A state backs an institute dedicated to advanced AI safety.
The institute evaluates frontier AI models.
Its work supports efforts to ensure those models are safe.
National institutes cooperate through an international network.
explainer.whyItMatters: AISIs place evaluation and safety work for the most advanced AI models within state-backed organizations. Their international network also creates a way for participating governments and the European Union to coordinate this work.
misconceptions: An AISI is a type of organization, not one single worldwide institute.
The term does not specify one particular safety test or evaluation method.
The UK and US institutes no longer use their original names.
